md_jungle_cliffs.blurb: Jungle Cliffs is one of the two main walls at Carderock, the small riverside crag on the Maryland side of the Potomac just outside Washington. The schist here is smooth and well polished, and it makes slick, technical climbing: steep prows, roofs, slabs and cracks, from first-time beginner routes up through hard 5.12 lines. Most of it is top-rope or short trad, with a few boulder problems mixed in. Trees back the cliff top, so bring a static line for anchors. Deciduous forest shades the wall, and the heavy foot traffic has buffed the holds, so the rock feels greasy when damp or in humid weather. The base is only a few minutes from the parking area, which makes it a popular after-work spot.
md_jungle_cliffs.parking_note: Use the north end of the Carderock parking area off the Clara Barton Parkway, then follow the trail west past the restroom building toward the river. Keep valuables out of your car, since break-ins have happened here.
md_jungle_cliffs.approach: From the lot, walk west past the toilets toward the river for a couple of minutes, then scramble down the second-class gully between Jungle Cliffs and the next wall over. The polished rock in the gully is slippery.

md_gateway_trail_boulders.blurb: A scattering of low faces, prows and boulders strung along the Gateway Trail in Catoctin Mountain Park, in the hills of northern Maryland. Nearly everything is a boulder problem, mostly overhangs and slabs, and the bulk of the problems fall between VB and V3 with a handful of harder lines up into the V5 to V8 range. A few short top-rope lines exist too. Many problems see few ascents, so expect some moss and dirt and a bit of route-finding between boulders. Bring pads for the trail walk, which is roughly a mile from the closest large trailhead lot, and stay off private land near the road. The hollow is shaded and damp, so it tends to climb best when it is cool and dry.
md_gateway_trail_boulders.parking_note: The usual start is the Lewis Property lot on Foxville Road (Route 77). A few spots at the roadside near the crag also exist, but leave the private campground nearby alone and keep your car clear of the road.
md_gateway_trail_boulders.approach: From the Lewis Property lot, follow the Gateway Trail for about a mile to the main concentration of boulders; the last stretch drops steeply and needs a short bushwhack. A longer alternative leaves the park headquarters and follows the creek east.

ma_rose_ledge.blurb: Rose Ledge is a string of short gneiss cliffs, roughly 40 to 60 feet tall, on Northfield Mountain above the Connecticut River. The rock is horizontally layered and mostly solid, with plenty of cracks and ledges for gear, so it is a favorite for learning to lead trad as well as for top-roping. Most routes run from 5.8 to 5.11, with easier lines on the lower tiers and a few much harder ones, and there are boulder problems below the cliffs. There are no sport routes. It is one of the busiest teaching crags in the region, so expect other parties on weekends. The walk in is a steady uphill hike on trails and woods roads of about 20 to 35 minutes depending on where you start.
ma_rose_ledge.parking_note: Most climbers use either the Northfield Mountain Visitor Center lot, which has the most room, or the small private lot on Poplar Mountain Road. Keep the dirt road clear and do not park on the shoulder.
ma_rose_ledge.approach: From the Poplar Mountain Road lot, walk uphill under the power lines and follow the trail signs toward the Rose Ledge trail, then turn up the gully with its stone steps. From the Visitor Center the walk is longer, via the Jug End and Rock Oak Ramble trails.

ma_mormon_hollow.blurb: Mormon Hollow is a compact gneiss crag in Wendell State Forest in western Massachusetts, a few miles from the better-known Farley Ledges. The rock is dense and clean, with good gear and sound anchors, and the climbing mixes slabs, technical faces, steep roofs and splitter cracks. Sport lines tend toward 5.10 and up, while the trad is mostly easier and well protected; a few hard boulder problems sit nearby. Most routes top out at around 65 feet, and bolted anchors make it easy to set up top ropes. It is quieter than Farley and trees shade the cliff in summer, but the roadside parking is tight and shared with neighbors, so park carefully and keep noise down.
ma_mormon_hollow.parking_note: Roadside parking is at the junction of Davis Road and Coldbrook Road in Wendell. Pull fully off the pavement and keep clear of field entrances and gates.
ma_mormon_hollow.approach: Follow the overgrown road uphill past the no-parking sign, then take the spur trail marked by a cairn to the base of the cliff. It is a short but steep climb.

mi_top_rope.blurb: The top-rope walls at Oak Park in Grand Ledge are the only sizable outdoor sandstone cliffs in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, standing 30 to 40 feet tall above the Grand River. The rock is soft and sometimes brittle, so gear never took hold here and the tradition is top-roping from tree anchors at the cliff top. Padding under the webbing keeps the lip from wearing. Routes range from easy 5.4 up into the 5.13s, with the greatest cluster in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. The wall faces south, so it is sunny and sheltered from wind; spring and fall are comfortable and summer is best early or late. Sandstone breaks more easily when wet, so wait out rain. Evenings and weekends can get busy.
mi_top_rope.parking_note: From downtown Grand Ledge, cross the river on Bridge Street, turn left on Front Street, and continue through the neighborhood to the dirt lot at the end of the road in Oak Park.

mi_cliff_drive_bouldering.blurb: Cliff Drive Bouldering gathers a few dozen problems on grey basalt in the woods of the Keweenaw Peninsula, near Ahmeek in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. The rock is mossy and quiet, and there is a good spread for a small area: plenty of V1 to V3, a solid run of V4 and V5, and a few harder lines above that. It is a low-traffic spot, so trails and some boulders can be overgrown, and ticks and poison ivy are around. Seepage can linger on the rock after rain. Land along Cliff Drive includes private property, so keep a low profile, follow the established trails and park out of the way of traffic. Bring pads and a spotter.
mi_cliff_drive_bouldering.parking_note: From Houghton drive north on US 41 through Calumet to Ahmeek, then turn left onto Cliff Drive. Pull off wherever the road allows without creating a hazard.

mi_rum_runner_s_cove.blurb: Rum Runner's Cove is a shoreline bouldering area on the south side of Lake Superior's cove near Wetmore Landing, east of Marquette. Boulders stand roughly 15 to 20 feet tall along the water, and the problems span VB up to V11, with most between V0 and V4 and a good number of harder lines for strong climbers. Nothing is bolted, so it is all pads and spotters, and landings are uneven and sometimes sloped, so bring several pads. Some lines are hard to spot, so expect to wander and look. The hike is long, and the lakeshore turns remote if weather shifts. Late spring through early fall is the usual window; wet shoulder-season rock gets slippery.
mi_rum_runner_s_cove.parking_note: Use the Wetmore Landing parking lot and walk toward the lake.
mi_rum_runner_s_cove.approach: From the parking lot, hike toward the lake, turn right before reaching the beach, and follow the blue blazes to the cove. Allow a good half hour or more each way carrying pads.

mi_main_wall.blurb: The Main Wall is the primary sport wall at Silver Mountain, a tall basalt cliff in Ottawa National Forest in the Upper Peninsula, southwest of Baraga. Most routes are bolted sport lines with stainless hardware, some stretching to two pitches, and there is a smaller amount of trad and a few boulder problems. Grades run from the 5.8s through 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.10s and 5.11s. Fall is the favorite season, when it is cool and the bugs are gone; spring brings seepage, mosquitoes and muddy forest roads, and summer is buggy and the dark rock can get hot. Facilities are minimal, so bring what you need.
mi_main_wall.parking_note: Reach the cliff by dirt forest roads: a two-track off Forest Road 922 leads to a small cul-de-sac used by climbers, or park at the Silver Mountain trailhead and walk along the base of the cliff.
